subject: Prospective PhD applicant (Fall 2027): what people think can be inferred from what they share
body:
Dear Prof. Li,

I'm an M.S. student in Data Science at Lakeshore University, and I'm applying to the Khoury HCI PhD program for Fall 2027. I'm writing because your lab's work is very close to the question that brought me to HCI. I'd love to know whether you're considering new students this cycle.

As a research assistant, I built bus ridership forecasting models using anonymized phone mobility data. While trying out features, I combined a rider's usual first boarding stop with where their phone tended to sit at night. Neither column identified anyone alone, but together they put many riders on just a few blocks. The feature didn't help the model, so I dropped it, and the data use was legitimate. Still, it left me wondering what people think can be figured out from what they share, and whether they could ever see it. That question feels more pressing now that people describe their lives to AI tools in their own words.

Your paper showing that agentic LLMs can re-identify participants in an anonymized interview dataset is that problem at a much larger scale. I'm especially drawn to the PEACH Lab's user-facing side, such as Rescriber and CIDER, which start from what people want to disclose and what they understand.

My background is mostly technical: a workshop paper on ridership forecasting, an industry data science internship, and a year as a transit data analyst. My first human-centered research was a small think-aloud study of an AutoML tool. In it, two participants assumed the tool already knew which columns were sensitive and would protect them. I'm applying for a PhD to get rigorous training in studying people, and to build on that.

I'd be happy to send my CV if helpful. If you're taking students, I'd be grateful for a short conversation, but I understand if your schedule doesn't allow it.

Best regards,
Morgan Reyes
M.S. Data Science, Lakeshore University
morgan.reyes@example.edu
